Still they steamed north.
The fleet numbered seven vessels: the Kaiyō, the Kaiten, the Banryū, the Shinsoku, the Chōgei, the Ōe, and the Hōō.
In the autumn of the year Boshin, on the thirteenth of the tenth month, the Enomoto fleet put into Miyako Bay, in the territory of the Nanbu domain, to take on firewood and water.
The ships threaded their way into the bay, whose channels were intricate.
"Ho-ho,"
said Toshizō, up on the Kaiyō's deck, narrowing his eyes at the splendor of the scenery about the bay.
"Ichimura Tetsunosuke,"
Toshizō called his page by his full name.
"Cold,"
said Toshizō.
Come the tenth month by the old calendar, the sea-wind of Ōshū had already turned chill.
Ichimura Tetsunosuke, sixteen years old and of the Ōgaki domain, brought Toshizō his greatcoat.
Toshizō, planting his long sword on the deck, hung the coat from his shoulders.

Miyako Bay lies in what is now the city of Miyako in Iwate prefecture, and has been made the Rikuchū Coast National Park. It is a so-called ria coast, rich in saw-toothed inlets, where the Kitakami Range falls to the sea in cliffs; seen from afar, the fishing villages are scattered along the tops of high sea-cut bluffs.
"Tetsunosuke, this is a feast for the eyes,"
said Toshizō.
Toshizō was full of hope. And not Toshizō alone.
Every soul in the Enomoto fleet had his heart quickened with the hope of the second Tokugawa dynasty they would build in Hokkaidō.
For that reason the scenery of Miyako Bay — likely their last port of call on the mainland — looked beautiful to every eye.

To set the scenery of this bay down as a picture, only a Western painting could do it, and that would take yellow from the tube in plenty. Every island, every cliff, was edged with strata of bright yellow and dark green.
"Matsushima too was beautiful, but it may not come up to this Miyako Bay,"
said Toshizō, more talkative than his wont, to Ichimura Tetsunosuke.
Hope was making the scenery beautiful.
"Yes, sir,"
answered the sixteen-year-old Ichimura, hugely pleased at his master's good humor.
The fleet went in slowly, taking soundings as it came.
The north bay was fairly wide. From the fishing village of Tachigasaki inward the water ran twenty fathoms deep, deep enough, but it shoaled by degrees the farther in one went. The bottom was mud.
The one fault of the north bay, though, was that it lay too open to the outer sea, and there was fear of wind and waves getting in; it could not be called a safe anchorage.
So Commander Enomoto judged.
The fleet went in as far as the front of a fishing village called Kuwazaki. Here the soundings ran from three fathoms to five.
For anchoring, more than enough.
And the lay of the land within the bay was intricate, and broke the wind.
──Here will do.

said Enomoto; but the inner bay was too cramped, and the whole fleet could not enter. Of necessity the two large ships, the Kaiyō and the Kaiten, dropped anchor in the lee of an island a little outside the mouth of that narrow stretch.
Watching how Enomoto handled the command, Toshizō raised his estimate of the man by degrees.
(He is capable, this one.)
What made him think so was the fineness of Enomoto's arrangements, and their care.

While he sent an envoy to the Nanbu domain, he did not for all that leave off the surveying of Miyako Bay. It was a thoroughness that verged on the obstinate. This Miyako Bay of Nanbu territory — once they had weighed anchor and gone, was it not a bay of no further use to them?
(Odd, that.)
Whether it was Enomoto's nature to begin with, or a way of doing things learned abroad, Toshizō could not tell.
"Enomoto, you are thorough indeed,"
said Toshizō, in the uniform of a French-style army officer, addressing Enomoto.
Enomoto wore a navy uniform of his own devising, which after his return from the Netherlands he had proposed to the old shogunate, and which had been adopted.

The stuff was black wool: a waistcoat, trousers, and over them a frock coat (though it could hardly be called that — it was a cross with the haori), all the buttons gold, with gold braid on the coat's sleeve to mark an officer's rank. Enomoto, ranking as full admiral, wore five.
Into the belt of those trousers he had thrust a Japanese sword, and he wore the figure-eight mustache he had grown while crossing over to Europe.
The mustache had been favored by the warriors of the Warring States, but through the three hundred years of the Tokugawa it had gone out of fashion.
Westerners, however, liked it. Enomoto's mustache might be called the badge of a Westernized shogunal retainer.

"At each port we put into, we survey with care and enter it on the chart, that guide of the sea-roads. Whether the port will be needed hereafter or not, we do it. It is a kind of habit, you might say, of a Western-style navy,"
Enomoto explained, kindly, for this unlettered swordsman's sake.
"Is that how it is."
Toshizō was thinking.
Into the head of this brawler there seemed to have risen a bizarre fancy such as Enomoto would never have had.
"Hijikata, what are you pondering?"

Enomoto asked, with keen interest. The commanders of the second Tokugawa dynasty's army were, every one of them, the choicest scholars and the ablest minds among the old shogunal retainers — only this Hijikata Toshizō was of another kind. And just for that, Enomoto took an interest in what this unlettered man of action would conceive.
"Well, Enomoto — you may laugh at me, but it is about this Miyako Bay. I am thinking of the case where the government fleet comes to raid Hokkaidō in time to come."
"Tell me — a steamship, how many days can she run at sea without putting in to any port?"

"It differs with the size of the ship, but when they form a fleet they set their pace by the smallest ship among them. A government fleet's transports would be two hundred tons at most, and if you loaded them full of land troops, they could not last three days on drinking water alone."
Enomoto had a touch of pedantry in him, too. He said things that were beside the point.
"As for speed of running,"
he went on,

"if you keep the boilers stoked and nothing more, even with good coal it is twenty days at most. To save that coal, on days when the wind serves you take pains to shut the boilers down and go under sail. To use those two powers skillfully is what makes a good captain, a good ship's master. Do it well, and you can run the open ocean for a month or so."
It was like sitting through a lecture.
But what Toshizō was after was something far more concrete.
"Enomoto — once the government fleet sets out from Edo Bay, it will surely put in here at Miyako Bay, will it not?"
"Ah, so that is your drift. Yes, they would put in."
"We strike them there,"
said the boss of the Shinsengumi.
"Eh?"

"Enomoto — only now do I see it, but a Western warship too seems to be an awkward thing. Once she drops anchor, she puts out the boiler-fires and lowers her sails; and so, at a cry of 'The enemy is upon us,' she cannot easily get under way. If, while the government fleet lies here at anchor, we suddenly came driving in with a warship of our own, the enemy would be wiped out to the last man."
"Ho — and then?"
Enomoto's eyes lit up.

"On our warship we keep our army aboard. If we can close without a gun-duel — that is, without so much as scratching the enemy's ships — lay ourselves against her side and go over the rail with the sword, why, the warship is taken whole, is she not?"
(Pff.)
Enomoto very nearly burst out laughing.
(The Shinsengumi is the Shinsengumi after all — the end of every talk is a sword-fight?)
So he thought; but unable to laugh, he gathered his strength into his tanden and said in dead earnest,
"A splendid notion."

This freak of a notion would later be realized as the Miyako Bay sea-fight of Toshizō and his men, a thing one might call all but unmatched in the history of the world's naval battles; but Enomoto, at this time, heard it out as, more or less, an amusing conceit.
The care of Toshizō's cabin and his person was in the hands of his page, Ichimura Tetsunosuke.
A slender-faced youth with clear, fresh eyes, he was, somewhere about the eyes, like Okita Sōji.
"You are like Okita."
Toshizō had once said so.
"Like Okita-sensei?"
This became Ichimura's pride.
That Ichimura was of the Ōgaki domain in Mino has been told already.
Just before the battle of Toba-Fushimi, when the Shinsengumi were quartered at the Fushimi magistracy, they held their last recruiting.
It was then that Ichimura, together with his elder brother Gōzō, deserted the Ōgaki domain and enlisted.

By the time they were taken on, Kondō and Okita, from wound and sickness, had already been sent back to Osaka. Toshizō was then the corps' captain in fact, and it was he who decided who was taken and who not.
When he looked at Ichimura Tetsunosuke, he was startled at how young in years he was.
"How old?"
he asked, and
"Nineteen,"
the boy lied.
Being sixteen now, he must have been fifteen then.
Toshizō only smiled a thin smile and said nothing.
"What school of the sword do you use?"
"I studied the Shintō Munen-ryū. I had come as far as the mokuroku, but with this upheaval I hold no seal of mastery."
"Cross swords with someone, then,"
and choosing the trooper Nomura Risaburō, he had them fence a match.
Neither was much good. But in fighting spirit Tetsunosuke had the better of it.
"You are like Okita. It does seem you have lied about your age, but for Sōji's sake I shall take you on,"
said Toshizō. As good as to say, it was thanks to Okita Sōji that he was taken.
For that one word Ichimura Tetsunosuke felt himself deeply in Okita Sōji's debt; and after the fighting at Fushimi, when they pulled back to Osaka, he met the bedridden Okita Sōji for the first time.
Okita said to Toshizō afterward,
"He is nothing like me,"
"Is that so."
Toshizō only smiled ruefully. There had been no great reason for saying such a thing at the time.
It was, after all, that Fushimi-magistracy time when he would have borrowed even a cat's paw.
(This one is too young.)
he had thought; but, well, never mind, and he took him. And then, as a reason to tell himself, Toshizō had
──He is like Okita; for that, I shall take him.
said no more than this.
That one word, one might say, shaped the whole life of Ichimura Tetsunosuke.

Ichimura, even aboard the Fujiyama-maru returning from Osaka to Edo, tended Okita without leaving his side; and with the one who mattered, the commander Kondō Isami, he was never in his whole life granted a word.
After they had returned to Edo, his brother Gōzō urged him,
──Tetsunosuke, let us run.
so he pressed.
Already the realm had turned against the Tokugawa, and the sharp-eyed for their own future were, night after night, slipping one away and vanishing two, out of the Shinsengumi.
Gōzō's flight, too, was no unnatural thing.

"Tetsunosuke, we are late-comers. To have fought at Fushimi is enough, I think. Stay in the corps beyond this, and now that the Satsuma and Chōshū men in Kyoto have raised the brocade banner, we become rebel troops,"
he said.
"No. I stay,"
said Tetsunosuke, newly turned sixteen, with a face brimful of conviction, and firmly.
"And your reason?"
"Tend Okita — that is what Hijikata-sensei told me to do."
"Eh?"
That was the whole of the reason.
Gōzō grew angry.
"Which is your brother — Okita Sōji, or I?"
"Brother — this is a hard case."
This feeling of his, none but himself could understand.
For Okita Sōji and he were alike.
"Because you are alike, I take you on."

So the vice-commander Hijikata Toshizō had plainly told him. And as for Okita Sōji, there was no one in Kyoto who did not know the name. Ichimura too, of course, had heard that thundering fame from afar. Surely the peerless swordsman the last days of the shogunate had brought forth, Ichimura had imagined the face and figure of Okita Sōji as a demon-like warrior.
Yet the real Okita Sōji, whom he faced in the sickroom at Osaka, was terribly bashful, used polite speech even to a stripling like Ichimura, and never once set him a task of his own accord.
Aboard the Fujiyama-maru, too,
"Ichimura. I am well, you know. Do not treat me so like an invalid,"
he would say.
On nights when the cough came, and Ichimura meant to sit up nursing him through the dark,
"Ichimura — you enlisted, did you, to turn me into an invalid? With you sitting there, little by little I come to feel like a sick man,"
he would say some such thing, and put him off.
There was no dealing with him.
Even after they were back in Edo, Ichimura would find spare moments from corps duties to go to the Medical Institute and nurse him, but,
"It will not do, Ichimura,"
he would laugh, with eyes much like Tetsunosuke's own, and,
"You are a boy, are you not. You did not join the Shinsengumi to nurse people, surely,"
he said.
Okita said it to Toshizō, too.
"That person—"
he said, meaning Ichimura Tetsunosuke,
"keep him from coming near me. I have a feeling it may be catching, and it puts me quite out of my mind."
Toshizō passed on Okita's words to Ichimura Tetsunosuke just as they were.
Tetsunosuke was overcome, and wept aloud. That a man like Okita should have thought so much of his welfare!
"That is just his disposition,"
Toshizō added; but to the young Ichimura Tetsunosuke it did not seem so.
(That it should be me.──)
and he trembled at the thought.
When his brother Gōzō urged him to flee, he had meant to give this as his reason for standing fast, but thought he would not be understood, and left off putting it into words.
To begin with, there was no way to express it. There is an old saying, a samurai dies for the man who knows his worth — but it was not quite that either.
Somehow, it was a strange thing.
Such strange, illogical, hazy things, and yet things charged with a kind of life, seem often to be the glue by which human beings are bound to one another.
"I stay,"
Tetsunosuke told his brother, flatly.
Gōzō, thereafter, went missing.
Tetsunosuke fought on with Toshizō, shifting from field to field, and on every battlefield was brave.
The reason was a simple one.
(I am like Okita.)
That, always, was his spur.

This man Ichimura Tetsunosuke afterward became one of the few survivors of the Shinsengumi; in the years after Meiji he lived out his life as nearly the sole teller of the tale of Hijikata Toshizō, and in Meiji 10 he enlisted in the Seinan War as a member of the Metropolitan Police corps, fought Saigō's Satsuma army, and was killed.
The Nanbu domain, in dread of the Enomoto fleet's power, handed over the supplies just as they were demanded.
Firewood was the chief thing supplied. Enomoto wanted coal, but in Ōshū that was not to be hoped for.
They settled for firewood in place of fuel, loaded her full, and sailed.
It was on the eighteenth of the tenth month that they left Miyako Bay. The day was fair, the waves somewhat high.
The fleet held on north. On the way they passed several foreign ships.
Each time, they ran up the shogunal war-flag, the Rising Sun.

The masters of those foreign ships knew well the intent of this fleet. For in the newspapers of the various nations put out from Yokohama, articles that Enomoto meant to set up a new government at Hakodate appeared almost daily.
